lines.speaker: detective
lines.text: His phone. Four digits. Three tries, then it locks for good.

lines.speaker: suspect
lines.text: Go ahead. You'll never guess it.

lines.speaker: reader
lines.text: It's not one two three four. You want people to think you're careful.
lines.say: It's not one, two, three, four. You want people to think you're careful.

lines.speaker: reader
lines.text: It's a date. People pick numbers they can't forget.

lines.speaker: reader
lines.text: Your ring. Engraved. Zero six, one four. Your wedding day.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: In 2012, a data analyst studied 3.4 million four-digit codes from leaked password lists.
lines.say: In twenty twelve, a data analyst studied three point four million four-digit codes from leaked password lists.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: The most common one, 1234, was almost eleven percent of all of them. The top twenty codes covered about a quarter.
lines.say: The most common one, one two three four, was almost eleven percent of all of them. The top twenty codes covered about a quarter.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: Right after the patterns come the dates. Birth years. Birthdays. Anniversaries.

lines.speaker: narrator
lines.text: And many of us reuse that same code for the phone, the bank card and the front door.

lines.speaker: reader
lines.text: We pick what's easy to remember. And what's easy to remember is easy to guess.

lines.speaker: reader
lines.text: So if your code is a date, a pattern, or a repeat, change it tonight.

lines.speaker: reader
lines.text: Six digits beat four. Random beats meaningful.

lines.speaker: reader
lines.text: And send this to the friend whose code is 1234.
lines.say: And send this to the friend whose code is one, two, three, four.
